entities.summary:
The Battle of Agincourt, fought on November 3, 1415, was a pivotal English victory in the Hundred Years' War against the combined forces of King Charles VI of France and his powerful ally, the Duke of Orleans. 

This turning point in the war marked a significant shift in the momentum of the conflict, as the English, led by King Henry V, emerged victorious against seemingly insurmountable odds, with a much smaller and more depleted force. 

The English longbowmen, armed with their trusty yew bows and arrows, played a key role in the English success, their tactical prowess and numerical superiority allowing them to outmaneuver and decimate the French knights. 

In the aftermath of this battle, the English continued their push into France, capturing key cities and fortresses, and setting the stage for the eventual Treaty of Troyes, which would recognize English control over large swaths of French territory. 

As historian David Hume noted, 'The whole course of the war was altered by the victory of Agincourt, and the English, who had been on the defensive, began to take the offensive.'

This 1415 English victory in the Hundred Years' War, at the cost of just 100 English soldiers and a reported 7,000 to 10,000 French casualties, left an indelible mark on the conflict, influencing the course of European history for centuries to come.
